rows.letter:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safer crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video under road-plane geometry and SAM tracking recorded 37.6 minutes (2256.0 s) at the Lantern Road crossing, observing 10 crossings and 6 vehicles.

In that short recording, 4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 10 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 12.2-73.8% and 2.5-55.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h.

The most severe near-miss involved a van at 58.7 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person had been on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 36.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.6%.

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.0 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

A further close pass involved a bus at 16.8 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%.

Engineering context, with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 37.6 minutes to 16 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles per hour, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 47.6% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 11.7 s, while the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
spark_problems: The letter claims the van passed after the person, but the measurements give no order for that event.

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Quarry Road crossing.

Our Crossing Watch video recorded 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.7 km/h. In that time 4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the serious events 1 was person-first and 3 were vehicle-first, and 1 close pass was also recorded.

One serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 56.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 13.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 0.8 s apart and involved a car at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss was 1.4 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6%, compared with 0.6% at 19.6 km/h.

A close pass was 2.4 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 43.6 km/h.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.0 minutes with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles counted, so we do not use that metric. About 72.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We ask for a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds toward the 20.0 km/h limit and provide priority. We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school about the crossing outside it on Hill View Road crossing. A video survey of 36.3 minutes (2178.0 s) recorded 38 crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 43.5 km/h.

In that time, 2 of 38 crossings (1 in 19) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. Both were serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and there were 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The most serious event was a van at 46.4 km/h just 0.4 s after the person had been on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% if hit at 20.0 km/h.

The second serious event was a van at 43.8 km/h just 0.6 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% if hit at 20.0 km/h.

For context, the recording gave PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 63 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.3 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and the method can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in a drone test). During the recording 62.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 2 gaps including 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 74.8 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce vehicle speeds toward 20 km/h and protect children and other users.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis of 8.6 minutes (516.0 s) of video recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

Of the 7 crossings, 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 3.7-71.0% and 3.7-71.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart), with 2 cases where the vehicle went first. 59.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, in 6 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 61.3 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video so this 8.6 minute sample is too short for those rates, and UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events were both classified as serious. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 55.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. The other involved a bus at 16.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, which would be 0.4% at an impact of 16.3 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Re: Safety at School Lane crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 mph zone markings at School Lane crossing.

A 5.6 minute video (336.0 s) at this crossing recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 41.1 km/h.
6 of 10 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s.
We note PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 5.6 minutes.
78.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst serious near-misses were as follows.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a bus at 42.4 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a car at 32.6 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a car at 15.4 km/h.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside Garden Road crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h approach markings. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

Crossing Watch video analysis covered 2.0 minutes (120.0 s). In that time 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 54.0 km/h. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. A close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 5 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts) would have been 9.7%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 9.1 km/h with a death risk of 0.2%.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 44.4 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 5.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

A third serious near-miss involved a bus at 27.8 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 1.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 20.6 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.6%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.1 km/h with a gap of 1.6 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 2.0 minutes. Also, 96.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 2 gaps of 6 s and 1 gap of 12 s or more. The longest gap was 69.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h approach markings to reduce approach speeds and protect pedestrians using the crossing.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements of the Bridge Street crossing undertaken with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time.

In 22.7 minutes (1362.0 s) there were 9 crossings and 29 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h.

Of the 9 crossings, 5 of 9 (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 9 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.2-86.3% and 7.5-70.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The most severe serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a motorcycle measured at 44.5 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 5.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van measured at 28.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.2%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car measured at 15.2 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 15.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a car measured at 44.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.0%.

The other close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a car measured at 37.7 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (24 pedestrians and 77 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.7 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 94.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and longest 60.2 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing. Most parents now avoid letting their children use the Bridge Street crossing alone because they consider it too dangerous.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians. Many pupils have to run across because drivers rarely slow down.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school about the crossing outside it on Hill View Road crossing. A video survey of 36.3 minutes (2178.0 s) recorded 38 crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 43.5 km/h.

In that time, 2 of 38 crossings (1 in 19) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. Both were serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and there were 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The most serious event was a van at 46.4 km/h just 0.4 s after the person had been on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% if hit at 20.0 km/h.

The second serious event was a van at 43.8 km/h just 0.6 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% if hit at 20.0 km/h.

For context, the recording gave PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 63 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.3 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and the method can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in a drone test). During the recording 62.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 2 gaps including 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 74.8 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce vehicle speeds toward 20 km/h and protect children and other users.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements for your review. The observation covered 36.3 minutes with 38 crossings and 10 vehicles.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of our school about the crossing on Station Road outside the school. We arranged a video survey of 15.2 minutes (912.0 s) which recorded 12 crossings and 32 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.0 km/h.

Of the 12 crossings, 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 15.2-72.3% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). The closest serious near-miss involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s at 45.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 5.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Another serious near-miss involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 41.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.0%. A third serious near-miss involved a bus with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (47 pedestrians and 126 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 15.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). Also 78.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and other pedestrians.

We would be happy to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your engineers to review. Please let us know how you will assess this site for safety improvements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The closest serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch video review at Market Street crossing. The video was 8.8 minutes (528.0 s) long and counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.7 km/h.

The review found 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart for serious and 1.5-3.0 s for close pass. The most serious involved a motorcycle at 55.9 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 13.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts. A second event was the closest near-miss, a close pass involving a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 8.8. Also 78.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 80.0 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Request for safety improvements at the Brook Street crossing

We write following a 4.5 minute (270.0 s) video recording at the Brook Street crossing, which captured 6 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles.

Headline findings were that 4 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 6 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. The recording also showed 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s).

In that recording the 85th percentile speed was 56.6 km/h.

Our most serious near-miss involved a van at 17.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 13.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

Our closest near-miss was a car at 51.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s.

Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

On engineering context, we note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.5. Also, 74.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 23.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given the speeds and the proportion of crossings with close vehicle interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We would be happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Ring Road crossing outside our school.

A 7.4 minute video (444.0 s) recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 43.4 km/h. Of the 3 crossings, 3 of 3 (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. In 2 cases the person was first and in 1 case the vehicle was first.

The closest serious near-miss involved a bus at 36.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In that case at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% death risk.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 29.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.5%. In that case at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% death risk.

A close pass involved a car at 41.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this recording is 7.4 minutes with 3 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. 53.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 44.9 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at School Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of 33.0 minutes of video at School Lane crossing, 29 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles were recorded with an 85th percentile speed of 56.7 km/h.

The review found 3 serious near-misses, defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. The pedestrian was first in 2 cases and the vehicle was first in 1 case.

The most severe was a van at 56.6 km/h with the closest post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.0% at 20 km/h where impact would be 0.0 km/h.

A second case was a car at 20.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A third case was a motorcycle at 18.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.5%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 53 pedestrians and 40 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 33 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. Also, 53.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 8 gaps including 8 of 12 s or more with the longest 32.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir or Madam,

At the Hill View Road crossing, Crossing Watch with SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded in 31.1 minutes 37 crossings and 9 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed of 56.0 km/h.

A close pass was 1.8 s apart with a car at 17.2 km/h, with 0.2% adult death risk, remaining 0.2% at 6.1 km/h impact.

The closest close pass was 2.4 s apart with a van at 20.6 km/h, with 0.0% adult death risk, remaining 0.0% at 0.0 km/h impact.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

rows.letter:
[School name]
[Date]

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table and 20 mph zone signs outside our school.

A 2.0 minute (120.0 s) video at the Synthetic example crossing (made-up tracks, no video) recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 3 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.0 km/h. Per the definition used, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). One serious near-miss involved a car at 38.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s. The other serious near-miss involved a car at 29.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s.

For an adult hit by a car front, the death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. For an adult hit at 38.0 km/h the death risk is 3.0%. For an adult hit at 29.0 km/h the death risk is 1.4%. At a 20.0 km/h impact the risk would be 0.6%.

Engineering context with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.0. Counted: 3 pedestrian crossings, 3 moving vehicles. 99.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 48.3 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request the raised zebra crossing with a speed table and 20 km/h zone signs to reduce vehicle speeds and increase gaps for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement data for your review.

Yours faithfully,

Head Teacher
